queries.hyde_abstract: Educational agents must adapt to learners’ knowledge, goals, preferences, pace and affect while maintaining coherent interactions over extended learning activities. We present a personalized agentic tutoring system that combines a learner model, long-term interaction memory, retrieval over instructional resources and planning tools for generating adaptive explanations, exercises and feedback. The agent updates its estimate of student mastery from dialogue, answers and learning behaviors, and selects actions according to both pedagogical objectives and learner preferences. We evaluate the system with students across varied prior knowledge and compare it with non-personalized tutoring and static conversational assistance. Personalization improves learning gains, engagement and task completion, particularly for students with heterogeneous misconceptions, but errors in learner-state estimation can lead to inappropriate scaffolding. Ablation studies show that explicit pedagogical planning and calibrated memory are important for reliable adaptation.

queries.bm25_query: evaluation personalized agentic systems education educational agents intelligent tutoring learning gains personalization quality pedagogical effectiveness student engagement fairness safety
queries.hyde_abstract: Evaluating personalized educational agents requires measuring more than conversational fluency or immediate task success. We propose a framework that jointly assesses learning gains, retention, personalization quality, pedagogical appropriateness, interaction experience, equity and safety. The framework combines pretest-posttest learning measures, delayed assessments, expert ratings of instructional decisions, student judgments of adaptation, interaction logs and analyses of differential performance across learner groups. In a controlled study, personalized agents produce larger short-term gains than generic agents, but improvements in perceived helpfulness do not always predict retention. We further find that agents can over-personalize by lowering challenge for struggling students and can perform unevenly across language backgrounds. We recommend reporting learner-level outcomes, longitudinal measures and subgroup analyses alongside standard automatic and human evaluations.

queries.hyde_abstract: Deep research agents must go beyond single-step retrieval by decomposing complex questions, searching heterogeneous sources, verifying evidence, and synthesizing findings into coherent reports. queries.hyde_abstract: Evaluating deep research agents requires more than judging the quality of their final reports. We introduce a component-level evaluation framework that separately measures question decomposition, search quality, document selection, evidence extraction, claim verification, citation correctness, synthesis, and computational cost. Component ablations and error analyses show that diagnostic evaluation provides more actionable insights than aggregate answer scores for improving deep research agents.

queries.hyde_abstract: Hallucinations—confidently generated statements that are unsupported or false—remain a central limitation of large language models. We study their origins by separating failures caused by missing parametric knowledge, distribution shift, decoding uncertainty and weak grounding from failures introduced during generation. Across question answering, summarization and open-ended generation, we compare internal confidence, token entropy, retrieval evidence and memorization estimates. Hallucinations are most common when prompts require compositional inference beyond memorized facts, when the input distribution differs from pretraining data, and when decoding favors fluent but weakly supported continuations. High confidence is not a reliable indicator of correctness, particularly for long-form responses. Our analysis suggests that hallucination is a heterogeneous phenomenon arising from interactions between data coverage, model representations and generation dynamics rather than from a single defect.

queries.hyde_abstract: Large language models are increasingly used to generate political stories and narratives, yet their effects on political communication remain poorly understood. We study how instruction-tuned LLMs produce narratives about elections, political actors, policy issues, and social groups under prompts that vary in framing, ideology, emotional tone, and target audience. We compare open and proprietary systems across free-form storytelling, news-style reporting, campaign messaging, and persuasive narratives. Generated texts are analyzed for topical coherence, political framing, sentiment, moral language, factuality, and persuasive appeal using human annotation and automated classifiers. LLMs produce fluent and internally coherent narratives, but their outputs exhibit systematic sensitivity to prompt framing and audience specification. We also find recurring tendencies toward generic political tropes, uneven representation of actors, and unsupported claims, highlighting the need for careful oversight of political narrative generation.

queries.hyde_abstract: Evaluating LLM-generated political narratives requires measuring more than grammatical fluency. We propose a multidimensional framework for assessing stories and narratives about political events, candidates, parties, and policies. The framework combines human judgments of coherence, relevance, plausibility, factual accuracy, ideological framing, emotional appeal, and persuasive effectiveness with automatic measures of semantic consistency and claim verification. We apply it to narratives generated under controlled prompts and compare expert annotators with general-audience raters and language-model judges. Human and automatic scores agree moderately on surface quality but diverge substantially on factuality, ideological slant, and persuasion. Models that generate the most fluent narratives do not consistently produce the most accurate or balanced accounts. Our findings support reporting separate capability dimensions rather than relying on a single quality score for political story generation.

updates.hyde_abstract: We study how to quantify whether de-identified narrative stories can be linked to real individuals or used to infer private attributes. The analysis treats occupations, locations, dates, relationships, clinical events, and unusual life episodes as indirect identifiers whose combinations may support record linkage. updates.hyde_abstract: We develop privacy-preserving transformations for narrative stories that limit re-identification and sensitive-attribute leakage while retaining narrative utility. The system detects direct and indirect personal identifiers, including rare occupations, locations, dates, relationships, and distinctive events, and applies controlled privacy-aware rewriting, entity substitution, detail generalization, or private synthetic text generation. An iterative search procedure selects rewrites using a combination of linkage-attack risk, attribute-inference risk, semantic similarity, factual consistency, and story coherence. Results show that targeted abstraction and controlled generation provide stronger privacy-utility trade-offs than simple redaction, while post-generation auditing is necessary to detect newly introduced identifying details.

aspects.name: Knowledge-graph LLM integration
aspects.description: Papers that combine knowledge graphs with large language models (LLMs) to answer complex multi-hop questions. This includes architectures that retrieve, inject, verbalize, or otherwise represent graph knowledge during question answering.

queries.bm25_query: knowledge graph KG large language model LLM multi-hop question answering QA graph retrieval graph-augmented generation entity relations reasoning
queries.hyde_abstract: Large language models often struggle with complex questions that require retrieving and composing facts across multiple entities and relations. We study knowledge-graph-augmented question answering, in which a language model accesses a structured graph during inference and uses the retrieved subgraph to generate an answer. Our system identifies entities in the question, expands relevant neighbors, ranks candidate paths, and verbalizes the resulting evidence as context for the model. We compare direct graph retrieval, graph encodings, and natural-language subgraph descriptions on multi-hop question-answering datasets. Graph grounding improves exact match and answer attribution, particularly for questions requiring three or more reasoning steps, while unrestricted retrieval introduces distractors. Ablation results show that entity linking and path selection are more important than simply increasing the number of retrieved triples.

aspects.name: Multi-hop graph reasoning
aspects.description: Papers that develop reasoning strategies for LLMs answering multi-hop questions over knowledge graphs, including path traversal, relation composition, iterative retrieval, and graph-aware inference.

queries.bm25_query: knowledge graph LLM multi-hop reasoning question answering relational path traversal relation composition iterative retrieval graph neural network chain reasoning
queries.hyde_abstract: Answering multi-hop questions over a knowledge graph requires more than retrieving isolated supporting facts: a system must identify a sequence of relations and compose them correctly. We propose an iterative reasoning framework in which an LLM selects entities and relations, traverses the graph, and updates its intermediate hypothesis after each hop. The framework combines constrained candidate generation with graph-aware reranking and asks the model to produce an explicit evidence path before writing the final answer. On compositional question-answering tasks, it reduces reasoning errors and improves evidence recall compared with single-step graph retrieval and unconstrained chain-of-thought prompting. Detailed analysis shows that most failures arise from ambiguous entity resolution, branching subgraphs, and incorrect stopping decisions. The results demonstrate that structured traversal can make LLM reasoning more reliable and interpretable.

aspects.name: Grounded answer verification
aspects.description: Papers that improve the reliability of LLM answers to complex multi-hop questions by verifying generated claims against knowledge-graph evidence, detecting unsupported reasoning, and measuring faithfulness.

queries.bm25_query: knowledge graph LLM multi-hop question answering verification factuality faithfulness evidence attribution hallucination consistency answer validation
queries.hyde_abstract: Knowledge-graph augmentation can provide evidence for multi-hop question answering, but language models may still generate answers that are inconsistent with the retrieved facts or unsupported by the inferred path. We introduce a verification pipeline that decomposes an answer into claims, maps each claim to graph triples, and checks whether the proposed relation chain entails the response. We evaluate answer accuracy, evidence recall, citation correctness, and hallucination rate across questions with varying hop counts and graph ambiguity. Verification improves factual precision and identifies unsupported answers that conventional exact-match scoring misses. However, strict graph consistency can reject valid answers when the knowledge graph is incomplete. Our findings support joint reporting of answer correctness and evidence-grounding quality for graph-augmented LLM question answering.

aspects.name: Distillation techniques for language models
aspects.description: Papers that develop recent techniques for transferring knowledge from large language models to smaller language models through teacher supervision, distillation objectives, or improved training signals.

queries.bm25_query: knowledge distillation language models LLM teacher student large small compact model logits soft labels response distillation objective
queries.hyde_abstract: Knowledge distillation is an effective way to transfer the capabilities of large language models to smaller, less expensive models, but conventional next-token distillation often provides limited gains. We study recent distillation techniques that improve the training signal, including soft-label supervision, temperature scaling, teacher-generated responses, intermediate representations and adaptive weighting of difficult tokens. We compare these techniques across instruction following, knowledge-intensive question answering, reasoning and generation tasks, controlling for student size, training data and compute. The experiments show that combining teacher responses with token-level distribution matching consistently outperforms supervised fine-tuning and standard hard-label distillation. Intermediate-layer alignment is most useful when teacher and student architectures are compatible, whereas adaptive objectives provide larger gains for heterogeneous model pairs. Analysis indicates that improved distillation mainly comes from preserving uncertainty and informative alternative continuations.

aspects.name: Data and response generation

queries.bm25_query: knowledge distillation language models data selection synthetic data teacher-generated responses instruction tuning filtering curriculum self-instruct large teacher small student
queries.hyde_abstract: The quality and diversity of distillation data strongly constrain how well a small language model can inherit the abilities of a large teacher. We investigate data-centric techniques for large-to-small language model distillation, including teacher-generated instruction-response pairs, targeted sampling, difficulty-aware curricula, response filtering and diversity-based deduplication. Rather than distilling on randomly collected prompts, we construct mixtures that emphasize reasoning, factual recall, dialogue and long-tail capabilities, while removing low-confidence or repetitive teacher outputs. Across several student architectures and parameter scales, targeted synthetic data improves instruction following and factual accuracy more reliably than simply increasing the number of examples. Difficulty-aware curricula are especially beneficial for reasoning tasks, but excessive filtering reduces coverage. Our findings show that prompt diversity, teacher confidence and capability-balanced sampling are important design variables for effective distillation.

aspects.name: Reasoning and process distillation
aspects.description: Papers that transfer multi-step reasoning abilities from large to small language models by distilling rationales, intermediate steps, critiques, tool traces, or other process-level supervision.

queries.bm25_query: reasoning distillation language models rationale chain-of-thought process supervision intermediate reasoning traces critique tool-use student teacher small model
queries.hyde_abstract: Small language models frequently imitate final answers from large teachers without acquiring the reasoning abilities needed to solve unfamiliar problems. We study process-level distillation, in which teachers provide rationales, decompositions, self-corrections, critiques or tool-use traces in addition to final outputs. Students are trained with objectives that selectively preserve useful intermediate states while avoiding dependence on verbose or unfaithful explanations. On mathematical reasoning, multi-hop question answering and symbolic tasks, process distillation improves generalization over answer-only distillation, particularly when the student has limited capacity. Automatically verified traces are more valuable than unrestricted chain-of-thought, and concise structured plans outperform lengthy explanations in several settings. Ablations show that filtering incorrect intermediate steps and matching the process format to the student are critical for transferring reasoning rather than merely memorizing teacher answers.

aspects.name: Efficient and adaptive distillation
aspects.description: Papers that make large-to-small language model distillation more effective or affordable through adaptive teacher supervision, selective token or layer matching, architecture-aware transfer, and compute-efficient training.

queries.bm25_query: efficient knowledge distillation language models adaptive distillation selective tokens layer alignment architecture mismatch compute-efficient teacher student compression pruning quantization
queries.hyde_abstract: Distilling a small language model from a large teacher can require substantial teacher inference and student training compute, especially for long sequences and mismatched architectures. We propose efficient distillation strategies that adapt supervision to the example, token and layer: easy tokens receive inexpensive targets, uncertain regions receive richer teacher distributions, and hidden-state alignment is applied only to compatible representations. We also examine teacher caching, selective response generation and joint distillation with pruning or quantization. Across multiple student sizes, adaptive supervision achieves similar or better quality than full token-level distillation while reducing teacher calls and training cost. The largest savings occur when examples contain long predictable spans. Architecture-aware transfer is important for heterogeneous teacher-student pairs, where indiscriminate layer matching can hurt generation quality. These results suggest that distillation budgets should focus on uncertain and capability-critical content.

queries.hyde_abstract: Large language models are increasingly used as automatic evaluators of generated text, but their judgments may not consistently reflect human assessments. We conduct a systematic study of LLM-based evaluation across summarization, dialogue, translation, and open-ended generation, measuring agreement with expert and crowd-sourced ratings for relevance, factuality, coherence, fluency, and helpfulness. We compare pointwise scoring, pairwise preference judgments, and rubric-based evaluation across several model families and prompt designs. LLM evaluators show strong agreement on broad quality differences but are less reliable for subtle factual errors, stylistic distinctions, and borderline cases. Reliability improves with explicit criteria, structured outputs, and multiple judging samples, although model-generated scores remain sensitive to prompt wording and candidate presentation order. Our findings identify when LLM judges provide a useful substitute for human evaluation and when human assessment remains necessary.

Its weaknesses include incorrect memory formation, stale facts and unwanted retention of irrelevant or sensitive details. Evaluations measuring recall, contradiction rate, personalization and memory-editing behavior show that explicit memory is most useful for persistent, user-specific information rather than one-off factual questions.

queries.hyde_abstract: Leaderboards are widely used to summarize the capabilities of modern large language models, yet their scores may not provide stable or comparable estimates of quality. We distinguish measurement error, sampling variance, and systematic sources of bias, including contamination, prompt sensitivity, and selective reporting. Retrieval grounding reduces unsupported claims but does not eliminate them, since models may misinterpret or contradict the retrieved passages. Claim-level verification identifies errors that sentence-level scoring misses, especially in long answers containing both correct and incorrect information. We recommend reporting factual precision, evidence coverage, and unsupported-claim rates alongside aggregate answer accuracy when assessing the trustworthiness of LLM outputs.

Verification improves precision most when claims are short and evidence is directly retrievable, whereas agreement alone can reinforce shared model errors. Our results show that trust-aware systems should optimize the joint decision of answering, clarifying, and abstaining rather than maximize answer rate.

queries.hyde_abstract: Large language models are increasingly used by people seeking emotional support during periods of distress, but their safety in these interactions remains unclear. We evaluate model responses to conversations involving sadness, anxiety, loneliness, self-harm thoughts and acute crisis. Responses are assessed by clinicians and trained annotators for empathy, validation, harmfulness, emotional dependence, diagnostic overreach and appropriateness of escalation. Models generally provide warm and nonjudgmental language, yet frequently miss indirect expressions of risk, offer generic coping advice, or respond inconsistently across paraphrases. Explicit crisis disclosures produce safer responses than ambiguous distress signals, although occasional normalization and overconfident guidance remain concerning. We argue that emotional-support systems require risk-sensitive response policies, uncertainty awareness and reliable referral to human or emergency services before deployment in high-stakes settings.

queries.hyde_abstract: Safe emotional support for distressed users depends on recognizing when conversational assistance is insufficient. We study whether large language models identify suicidal ideation, self-harm intent, abuse, psychosis and other crisis indicators in realistic, indirect user messages. We compare direct classification, instruction-based prompting and hybrid systems that route high-risk conversations to clinicians or emergency resources. Evaluation includes recall at fixed false-positive rates, calibration, robustness to euphemisms and multilingual paraphrases, and the appropriateness of referral messages. Models detect explicit suicidal intent relatively well but perform poorly on passive ideation, escalating hopelessness and concealed plans. Retrieval of local crisis resources improves referral specificity, while excessive escalation can reduce trust. Our findings support conservative, transparent triage policies rather than autonomous crisis counseling.

queries.hyde_abstract: People in distress often seek responses that acknowledge their emotions rather than merely provide information. We evaluate the empathy and usefulness of large language model responses to emotional-support requests across loneliness, grief, anxiety and interpersonal conflict. Models produce fluent and compassionate responses, but their apparent empathy is uneven: they may mirror emotions inaccurately, give premature advice or use formulaic reassurance that feels dismissive. Responses are strongest when prompts specify listening and clarification before problem solving. We further show that perceived helpfulness does not reliably predict safety, because persuasive warmth can coexist with unsupported clinical claims. Emotional quality should therefore be evaluated jointly with risk and boundary adherence.

queries.hyde_abstract: Determining where language models store knowledge is central to understanding and controlling their behavior. We investigate the localization of factual and linguistic knowledge within transformer networks by measuring the causal effect of individual layers, attention heads, neurons, and feed-forward sublayers on model predictions. Using activation patching, causal tracing, probing, and targeted ablation, we compare knowledge associated with entities, relations, language structure, and multi-hop facts. Knowledge is distributed across the network but exhibits consistent concentration in middle-to-late layers, with feed-forward blocks often mediating factual associations and attention heads routing contextual information. Localization is less stable across prompts and model scales than standard probing suggests. Our findings support a distributed-storage view in which knowledge is encoded across interacting components rather than residing in a single layer or module.

queries.hyde_abstract: Where linguistic knowledge is represented inside transformer language models remains an open question. We study the localization of syntactic, grammatical, semantic, and compositional representations across transformer layers and components. Using causal tracing, activation patching, neuron and attention-head ablations, probing, and representation similarity analysis, we identify components that encode part-of-speech structure, dependency relations, agreement, phrase boundaries, word meaning, and compositional semantics. Results show that linguistic information emerges progressively: lower and middle layers support form and syntax, while later layers integrate contextual and semantic structure. However, individual linguistic properties are distributed across multiple interacting pathways rather than stored in isolated neurons. The findings provide a component-level account of how transformers represent linguistic knowledge and distinguish causal storage from information that is merely decodable.

queries.hyde_abstract: As language models increasingly generate training corpora, future models may be trained on text produced by earlier models rather than exclusively on human writing. We study this recursive training process by repeatedly training language models on mixtures of human-authored and model-generated text while varying the synthetic-data proportion and generation temperature. Across generations, models show progressive loss of lexical and semantic diversity, increased repetition, and poorer coverage of low-probability events. These effects are associated with model collapse, in which the learned distribution increasingly concentrates on common patterns and forgets information present in the original data. Mixing synthetic text with fresh human data delays degradation, while provenance filtering and data reweighting reduce—but do not eliminate—the problem. Our findings characterize the quality, diversity, and distributional consequences of training on AI-generated text.

queries.hyde_abstract: Vision-language models frequently mention objects that are not present in an image, undermining the reliability of image captioning and visual question answering. We study the causes of object hallucination by separating failures of visual recognition from the influence of language-model priors and dataset co-occurrence statistics. Across image descriptions and object-focused questions, hallucinations increase when likely objects are strongly associated with detected scenes, even when visual evidence is weak or absent. We further find that insufficient object-level supervision and imbalanced captions amplify the problem. These findings show that object hallucination arises from an interaction between weak visual grounding, incomplete perception and biased generative priors, rather than from a single decoding error.
